## Solution

**Answer: False.**

### Proof

The statement claims that every curve of constant width must be a finite union of arcs of circles. We show this is false by exhibiting (indeed, by showing the abundance of) curves of constant width that are not finite unions of circular arcs.

**Background on constant-width curves via support functions.**

A convex curve of constant width $w$ can be described by its support function $h(\theta)$, where $h(\theta)+h(\theta+\pi)=w$ for all $\theta$. The radius of curvature is
$$\rho(\theta) = h(\theta) + h''(\theta),$$
and it satisfies
$$\rho(\theta) + \rho(\theta+\pi) = w, \qquad \rho(\theta) > 0.$$
Conversely, given any positive, sufficiently smooth function $\rho$ on $[0,2\pi)$ satisfying $\rho(\theta)+\rho(\theta+\pi)=w$, one obtains a (smooth) curve of constant width $w$.

**Key observation.** A circular arc has *constant* radius of curvature. Therefore, a curve that is a finite union of arcs of circles has a radius of curvature $\rho(\theta)$ that is piecewise constant (constant on each arc, with jumps at the finitely many junction points).

**Constructing a counterexample.**

Choose any smooth, strictly positive function $f:[0,\pi]\to(0,w)$ that is *not* constant on any subinterval — for instance,
$$f(\theta) = \tfrac{w}{2} + \tfrac{w}{4}\sin\theta, \qquad \theta\in[0,\pi].$$
Extend to $[0,2\pi)$ by setting $\rho(\theta+\pi) = w - f(\theta)$, i.e.,
$$\rho(\theta) = \begin{cases} \tfrac{w}{2}+\tfrac{w}{4}\sin\theta & 0\le\theta<\pi,\\ w-\bigl(\tfrac{w}{2}+\tfrac{w}{4}\sin(\theta-\pi)\bigr) = \tfrac{w}{2}-\tfrac{w}{4}\sin(\theta-\pi) & \pi\le\theta<2\pi. \end{cases}$$
This $\rho$ is smooth, strictly positive, and satisfies $\rho(\theta)+\rho(\theta+\pi)=w$. It therefore defines a smooth curve of constant width $w$.

Since $\rho(\theta)=\tfrac{w}{2}+\tfrac{w}{4}\sin\theta$ is a *non-constant analytic function* on $(0,\pi)$, it is not constant on any open subinterval. Hence $\rho$ is not piecewise constant — it is not even locally constant anywhere except at isolated critical points.

**Why this rules out a finite union of circular arcs.** A finite union of circular arcs yields a radius of curvature that is piecewise constant with finitely many pieces. Such a function is constant on each of finitely many open intervals covering the circle (up to finitely many points). Our $\rho$ is non-constant on *every* open subinterval of $(0,\pi)$, so it cannot coincide with any piecewise-constant function with finitely many pieces. Therefore the resulting curve of constant width is **not** a finite union of arcs of circles.

**Remark.** This is not a pathological isolated example: the space of smooth constant-width curves is infinite-dimensional (parametrized by an arbitrary smooth positive function on $[0,\pi]$ with the single constraint above), whereas finite unions of circular arcs form a finite-dimensional family. Thus "generic" curves of constant width are not finite unions of circular arcs. The Reuleaux triangle and its polygonal generalizations (Reuleaux polygons) are special, highly non-generic members of the class.

### Conclusion

There exist curves of constant width that are not finite unions of arcs of circles. The statement is **False**.

### PROOF COMPLETE
